issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies an interpersonal/home-intrusion threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items, which center on contamination/body danger and intrusive sensory reliving.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' is not impossible after chemical exposure, but here it reads as preparation for assault/entrapment rather than avoidance of fumes, contamination, or bodily symptoms; it is weakly aligned with the rest of the profile and the trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items focus strongly on social/cultural disconnection and not belonging, which is difficult to reconcile as the central appraisal pattern for a 60-year-old male whose trauma was toxic chemical exposure. These appraisals are not impossible, but alongside the rest of the profile they are poorly connected to the main symptom pattern of somatic threat, false alarms, and sensory reliving. A clinician would question why chemically exposure-related PTSD is expressed mainly as community/cultural alienation rather than danger, contamination, mistrust of body, or permanent harm beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the profile is dominated by body-based threat and intrusive sensory memory, but the maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others' is not well supported because the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from all other nodes. Reminder-based avoidance centered on external prompts by others implies a trigger-driven maintenance pattern that is not reflected in the formulation or elsewhere in the self-report.

vignette: Duy had been inspecting the chemical storage cart in the hotel’s mechanical basement when the pressure valve sheared. A thick plume of acrid vapor rolled across the concrete floor, catching in his throat and coating his tongue with a sharp, metallic tang. He remembered stepping back, the alarm beginning to wail, the way the heavy air seemed to press against his chest. When the maintenance crew opened the door and pulled him into the hallway, that specific flavor remained. Over the following weeks, the taste forced its way into his mind unbidden, usually during the quiet hours after his shift. He would close his eyes and feel as though the vapor were still rising around him, as if the exposure were happening right then rather than months ago. He had come to believe that his own body had betrayed him; it had taken in the wrong thing, and now it no longer felt entirely his own. As the months passed, Duy’s vigilance tightened alongside his quiet dread. His body remained coiled, perpetually tense and ready to react even when the lobby was empty. He found himself scanning the ceilings and vents whenever he walked through the corridor, his eyes moving steadily across the architecture, looking for any sign of trouble. When a guest complaint took longer than expected to resolve at the front desk, he was certain that something was wrong beneath the surface, his pulse quickening as though a delay signaled an impending collapse. He began reacting to ordinary sounds—a dripping coffee machine, a rolling luggage cart, the low hum of the ice maker—as if danger were already present. Checking his own pulse, his breathing, his shoulders for tightness, he monitored his frame constantly, waiting for the first clear sign of injury. He could not stop bad things from arriving, and he felt increasingly unmoored, as though the hotel he had managed for twelve years no longer belonged to him, and neither did his own home. To keep the discomfort at bay, Duy started avoiding the reminders that came in conversation. When staff members mentioned the basement storage, or when his partner asked about the renovation chemicals, he would nod quietly and steer the dialogue toward scheduling or inventory. The habit deepened as weeks turned into months. At work, he began delegating the routine chemical checks to his assistant manager, his hands tightening around his coffee mug when the delivery trucks idled outside. His partner noticed how his shoulders remained raised when they walked together, how he would pause on the sidewalk to look up at the neighboring buildings, ensuring the air felt clear. His avoidance settled into a quiet rhythm, narrowing the spaces where he could move without constant scrutiny. Now, sitting in a corner of the hotel’s conference room during a weekday lull, Duy watches the staff move through the glass doors. His intake questionnaire scores sat at sixty-eight, but the numbers only partially captured the weight of his days. He has finally scheduled the appointment because the false alarms have begun to interrupt his meals, and the uncontrolled memories are making it difficult to rest. He is most afraid of the moment when his body will no longer signal what is real, of the quiet assumption that something will break before he can intervene. Yet, as he prepares to leave for the clinic, he is hoping that someone might help him understand why his frame feels so heavy, and perhaps, how to stay where he is without constantly looking for what might go wrong.
